paper_title: Sharpen Without Search: On-Policy Distillation of Sequence-Level Power Distribution

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: A language model can give a correct answer more probability than any single incorrect answer and still usually sample an incorrect one, because the incorrect answers together hold more probability. The power distribution raises each complete answer's probability to a power above one and renormalizes, shifting probability toward answers the model finds most likely (sharpening). Sampling from it improves reasoning without changing parameters, but needs many scored candidates per query. We show that a model can instead be trained to produce such answers in one generation. On-policy power distillation (OPPD) runs a sequential Monte Carlo sampler in which the model being trained generates candidates and a frozen teacher's power distribution weights them; the same probabilities weight each answer in a maximum-likelihood update. Training raises single-generation accuracy by up to 23.0 points on MATH500 and 27.3 on GSM8K over the untrained model at the same temperature, and one generation scores 2.4 and 3.5 points above published power sampling with 64 candidates, recovering 94 percent of the gain that 16 candidates give the untrained model. For context, against GRPO trained with verified rewards from the same checkpoint and budget, OPPD scores 3.8, 4.0 and 5.4 points higher on MATH500, GSM8K and AIME using no reference answers; the two are complementary, and OPPD applied after GRPO adds up to 9.3 points. Trained only on mathematics, OPPD raises HumanEval accuracy by up to 5.3 points. One loss coefficient moves the sharpening exponent the model absorbs between 1.19 and 2.02, against 1.14 for ordinary on-policy distillation, and it rises mostly on the model's own answers. Gains hold across model families and sizes, including a model already trained with verified rewards, where lowering the temperature gives nothing and OPPD adds 4.4 points on MATH500. Code: https://github.com/ArminAzizi98/OPPD.

(Karan & Du, 2026; Ji et al., 2026). On 250 MATH500 problems, Qwen2.5-Math-7B scores 66.8% when it generates one answer and 79.2% when sampler with sixteen candidates draws approximate samples from πα. This sampler, however, has to run again for every query. In this paper we ask whether this cost can be paid once, during training. Ordinary distillation trains student to match teachers next-token probabilities. The next-token probabilities of πα, however, depend on all possible continuations of the prefix, so no teacher forward pass computes them. Samples from πα can therefore only be drawn approximately, by sampler run at inference time. Our method, on-policy power distillation (OPPD), trains the student on the output of such sampler, the sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) sampler of Azizi et al. (2026). This sampler extends candidate answers in blocks of tokens and gives each candidate an importance weight, which measures how much more probable it is under πα than under the distribution that generated it. When these weights become too uneven, it replaces low-weight candidates with copies of high-weight ones. In OPPD the student generates the candidates and frozen teacher defines πα; in self-distillation, the teacher is copy of the initial student. The teacher probabilities that set the importance weights also give each complete answer training weight, and the student is updated by weighted maximum likelihood on its own answers (Figure 1). second loss term, the token-level anchor with coefficient λ, keeps the students next-token distributions near those of the teacher at temperature 1/α. sections.title: 4 MEASURING ABSORBED SHARPENING
sections.content: Higher accuracy alone does not show that the student moved toward πα, so we test consequence that is specific to this movement. Let pbase be the model the student was initialized from, and let context be prompt with prefix. If training sharpened the student relative to pbase with some exponent a, so that pϕ base/Z, then log pϕ(v c) = log pbase(v c) log Z(c), (10) which is line of slope in log pbase(v c) at each context c. slope of 1 means that no sharpening was absorbed, and slope of α means that the student equals pbase at temperature 1/α. We estimate the slope by least squares of log pϕ on log pbase over the 200 tokens most likely under pbase, weighted by pbase(v c) so that the near-zero tail does not dominate. We report the median slope across contexts as the absorbed exponent αeff (pbase pϕ). In self-distillation αeff (pbase pT) = 1.000 exactly, so no measured increase can come from copying sharper model; with larger teacher, the control is ordinary on-policy distillation against the same teacher. The slope is dominated by noise when pbase is close to deterministic, so we report αeff only where the entropy of pbase is large enough for the fit to separate the models, and direct entropy measurement elsewhere. Appendix gives both and validates the estimator on synthetic logits.

sections.title: 5 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: Setup. Our main experiments use Qwen2.5-Math-7B (Yang et al., 2024) in self-distillation, which makes the control of Section 4 exact. We repeat the training on Qwen3-8B-Base (Yang et al., 2025), Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024), Qwen3-14B-Base and deepseek-math-7b-rl (Shao et al., 2024), and use Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B as the student for the sweep over λ. Training prompts are GSM8K questions (Cobbe et al., 2021) except in Appendix B.12, and no reference answer is used in training. We set α = 4, increased linearly from 1 over the first 20% of steps, with = 16 candidates, blocks of = 64 tokens, resampling when the ESS falls below N/2, and β = 0.7. Training runs for 300 steps at two prompts per step (Appendix J). We generate four answers per problem for 200 problems each from GSM8K and MATH500 (Lightman et al., 2024), graded with the reference power-sampling implementation. We do the same for AIME 2024 and 2025 pooled (60 problems, 3500-token limit; 4096 for Qwen3-14B-Base). pass@1 is the fraction of the four answers that are correct, averaged over problems, and best-of-4 counts problem solved if any answer is correct. The paired standard error on pass@1 difference is about 2.9 points. Our baseline is ordinary on-policy distillation against the teacher at temperature 1/α, which is (9) with the anchor alone and no training weights or resampling. Our measurements of the untrained model are within 3 points of published numbers, in both directions (Appendix K). Qwen2.5-Math-7B improves under many training signals, including rewards uncorrelated with correctness (Shao et al., 2025), so the replications on other families in Section 5.4 carry as much of the claim as this model does. 5.1 ACCURACY Generating one answer at temperature 1/α, the model trained with OPPD scores 2.4 points above published power sampling with 64 candidates on MATH500 and 3.5 points above it on GSM8K  (Table 1)  . Two further seeds score 79.50 and 81.25 on MATH500, so every run exceeds published power sampling (Appendix B.2). At temperature 1, this model gains 23.0 and 27.3 points over the untrained model and 11.0 and 11.6 points over ordinary on-policy distillation. Best-of-4 also rises on both benchmarks, so the model solves more problems rather than repeating the same answer. Lowering the temperature to 1/α requires no training, so comparing models at that temperature separates the contribution of training from that of decoding. At this temperature, ordinary on-policy distillation loses 1.9 and 1.8 points relative to the untrained model, both within one standard error, while OPPD gains 8.4 and 15.0. The single-answer result also matches published GRPO on MATH500, 78.5 against 78.0  (Table 1)  . The published numbers come from different evaluation protocol. Under ours, on the same 250 problems, the sixteen-candidate sampler scores 79.2 and OPPD 78.4  (Table 9)  . On 250 MATH500 problems, sixteen candidates add 12.4 points for the untrained model, of which OPPD obtains 11.6 (94%) with single generation. Running the sampler on the trained model adds only 1.6 more (Appendix B.1).

We train the two methods from the same checkpoint to put OPPD on that scale, not to argue that one should replace the other, and they compose. We train OPPD and GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) from the same Qwen3-8B-Base checkpoint for 300 optimizer steps each. At each step, both draw two prompts and sample sixteen answers of at most 1024 tokens per prompt, so each generates 9,600 answers. Our GRPO is the standard version, with one optimization pass over each batch of samples and binary reward from the evaluation grader. Both runs are small next to published GRPO training, 600 prompt draws of at most 1024 tokens each, so the comparison bounds neither method at larger budget. OPPD scores higher on all three benchmarks  (Table 13)  , by 3.75 points on MATH500, 4.00 on GSM8K and 5.42 on AIME, each between one and two standard errors and all three with the same sign. GRPO learns only from groups of answers whose rewards differ, and 234 of the 600 groups (39%) gave every answer the same reward and no gradient, while every prompt drawn produced gradient for OPPD (Appendix B.10). The two methods also combine. sections.title: 6 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Power sampling and sequential Monte Carlo. Karan & Du (2026) introduce Metropolis Hastings sampling from the power distribution (1) and show that it matches reinforcement-learning post-training on reasoning benchmarks. Azizi et al. (2026) replace the serial Markov chain with the batch-parallel sampler we use, and Ji et al. (2026) approximate the next-token distribution of πα with sampled continuations. All three methods run at inference time. Tomihari & Sato (2026) show that the power distribution is the closed-form optimum of KL-regularized reinforcement learning when the reward is the models own sequence log-probability, and derive power self-distillation, which trains model on samples power sampler produced and reaches accuracy at or above power sampling at much lower inference cost. Moving the cost of power sampling into training is therefore established. OPPD differs in where the training answers come from and in what is optimized: the student is the samplers proposal distribution, so the answers are its own and one teacher pass per block serves both the sampler and the update, and the objective is the Renyi family (3) rather than supervised learning on stored samples. OPPD trains on-policy, the setting for which on-policy distillation was introduced (Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024). SMC has also been used to steer language models toward constraints (Lew et al., 2023) and for inference with learned twist functions (Zhao et al., 2024), and Hu et al. (2024) learn to sample intractable posteriors with GFlowNet objectives. We do not learn twist function (Section 2.2). Distillation and post-training. Sequence-level knowledge distillation trains student on answers generated by the teacher (Kim & Rush, 2016; Hinton et al., 2015), and on-policy variants train on answers the student generates and the teacher scores. Methods that use verified rewards, such as GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), need to know whether each answer is correct. Methods that reward models own confidence instead include entropy minimization (Agarwal et al., 2025), self-certainty (Zhao et al., 2025), negative token entropy (Prabhudesai et al., 2025) and majority-vote rewards (Zuo et al., 2025), and Huang et al. (2025) analyze self-improvement as sharpening against the models own judgments. With the proposal of Theorem 1 and β = 1, (5) makes our training weight softmax over the negative Renyi entropy accumulated along each answer, confidence weighting whose scores come from frozen teacher and are used inside sampler. OPPD needs only the questions, so it applies where those methods cannot be run, and it can also be applied to model those methods have already trained. Yue et al. (2025) argue that such methods mostly re-weight answers the model could already produce, as power sampling does.

sections.title: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.content: OPPD trains model toward the sequence-level power distribution of teacher, so that one generation replaces the sampler. The trained model scores above published power sampling with 64 candidates, matches GRPO trained from the same checkpoint and budget without reading reference answers, and improves model that verified rewards have already trained. One loss coefficient controls the sharpening.

This shows that the two can be combined, but it does not say how large the gain from OPPD is beside method that reads reference answers. Here we train both ourselves, from the same starting model and with the same budget. The comparison uses one standard implementation of GRPO at one budget, and we draw no conclusion from it about the wider family of reinforcement-learning methods that use verified rewards. What is held equal. Both methods run for 300 optimizer steps. At each step both draw two prompts and sample sixteen answers of at most 1024 tokens per prompt, so each method generates 9,600 answers over the run. GRPO additionally uses reference answer for every training question, which OPPD never does. Our GRPO implementation is the standard one, with single optimization pass over each batch of samples. For each prompt it samples sixteen answers, called group, and scores each with binary reward from the grader used for evaluation. The advantage of each answer is its reward minus the group mean, divided by the group standard deviation. With single pass, the model that generated the samples is the model being updated, so the ratio between the new and the sampling probabilities is one and the clipping range is inactive. OPPD scores higher on all three benchmarks (Figure 6), by 3.75 points on MATH500, 4.00 on GSM8K and 5.42 on AIME. Each margin is between one and two standard errors, so none is conclusive on its own, but all three favor the method that uses no reference answers. AIME has only 60 problems, so the pass@1 margins there are imprecise. Groups that give GRPO no training signal. GRPO learns from group only when the rewards in it differ. If all sixteen answers earn the same reward, the group mean equals every reward, all advantages are zero, and the prompt contributes no gradient. Our logs record how often this happened: 234 of GRPOs 600 prompt draws (39%) had uniform rewards and produced no gradient. These draws still cost computation, because the answers had to be generated before their rewards could be compared. This fraction is higher than the average reward rate would suggest. Late in training, the mean reward ranged from 0.06 to 0.97 across steps. If every answer succeeded independently at the average of these rates, fewer than 2% of groups of sixteen would have uniform rewards. Observing 39% therefore means that difficulty is not spread evenly across prompts. given problem tends to be either easy for the model, so that most of the sixteen answers succeed, or too hard, so that almost none do. Both cases tend to give uniform rewards and zero advantages, so mainly problems of intermediate difficulty provide learning signal. OPPD does not have this problem, because its training weights come from the teachers probabilities rather than from correctness check. Sixteen answers that are all incorrect still differ in the total probability the teacher assigns them, so their training weights still differ. The measured ESS stayed between 0.39N and 0.64N throughout training, so no groups weight concentrated on single candidate, and every prompt drawn produced gradient. The two methods also place different requirements on the training data. GRPO needs reference answer that grader can check, and of the 12,000 OpenR1-Math-220k items we examined, 8,236 had one. The rest give their answer in form that the grader cannot match to single expression, such as pair of values or multiple-choice letter. OPPD uses only the question, so all 12,000 items were available to it. B.11 RESULTS ON AIME MATH500 and GSM8K are solved often enough by the untrained model that large part of each score is already available before training. We therefore also evaluate on AIME, competition benchmark on which 7B model rarely succeeds. We pool the 2024 and 2025 problem sets, giving 60 problems, and generate four answers for each. All rows use the same 3500-token generation limit, which keeps the prompt and the answer inside the models context window. The untrained model solves 4.17% of AIME problems on single attempt. Training it with GRPO on verified rewards raises that to 10.83%, and OPPD, which uses no reference answers, reaches the same 10.83% (Figure 5). The two methods reach this number with different requirements: GRPO needs to know whether every training answer was correct, while OPPD needs only the questions. Applying OPPD after GRPO exceeds either method alone, reaching 12.92%. Best-of-4 separates the three more clearly, at 21.67 for GRPO, 20.00 for OPPD, and 31.67 for the two together. The combined model solves 31.67% of these problems within four attempts, where the untrained model solves 13.33%, so it solves problems that the untrained model does not solve in four attempts. Selecting among answers the untrained model already produces cannot give such gain. The AIME result holds on second model. We repeated the evaluation on Qwen3-8B-Base, stronger and more recent starting point than Qwen2.5-Math-7B. The untrained model solves 7.08% of AIME problems on single attempt, and OPPD raises that to 14.17%, with best-of-4 going from 16.67 to 26.67. Single-answer accuracy at least doubles on both models, and 14.17% is the highest AIME result among our 7B and 8B models, so the pattern does not depend on starting from model that rarely solves these problems.

sections.title: P CORRECTING THE WEIGHT ADVANTAGE OF STOPPING EARLY
sections.content: Equation (5) implies that the log importance weight decreases at every token. candidate that emits the end-of-sequence token keeps its weight fixed while unfinished candidates continue to lose weight, so stopping early gains weight for reasons unrelated to answer quality. For long chains of reasoning, this would train the model to stop reasoning early, and the loss curve would give no sign of it. We charge each finished candidate the mean per-token increment in log importance weight of the unfinished ones. This is the same constant for every finished candidate at given step, so the normalized weights among unfinished candidates are unchanged, and only the comparison between finished and unfinished candidates is corrected. As diagnostic, we use the mean answer length weighted by the normalized importance weights minus the unweighted mean length, which should be near zero. We measure this diagnostic in controlled setting where student and teacher are the same model, so that the per-token decrease is identical across candidates and any preference for length comes from the weight accounting: weighted minus unweighted length ESS/N without the correction with the correction 25.9 tokens +0.13 tokens 0.084 0.

sections.title: Q RESAMPLING AND THE TRAINING WEIGHTS
sections.content: Resampling duplicates candidates. The training weights already recorded for earlier blocks are stored per candidate, so duplicated candidate carries its ancestors recorded weight once per copy. Without correction, the total training weight on an earlier block grows with every resampling step (a block that survives steps is amplified by up to k), and the opening tokens of every answer come to dominate the loss. Neither the loss value nor any standard diagnostic shows this. Duplication is how resampling represents weight, so the recorded training weights must be renormalized to compensate. After each resampling step, we renormalize the stored training weights of every earlier block to sum to one across candidates. The test suite of Appendix checks this property automatically. The sampler and the loss also keep separate weight accumulators. The samplers accumulator uses (2) and decides when to resample. Replacing it with the training weight, which depends on β, would stop the sampler from approximating πα. The loss accumulator uses (8), is reset at every block boundary, and supplies A(i). Their per-token increments agree at β = 1, but for every β they accumulate over different windows. We write the training weight with the letter to keep it distinct from the importance weight .
